data.title: ANT, META Stock Slip After-Hours Amid Reports That Apple Is Working On Its Own AI Agent
data.description:
Key points:
  • Apple’s effort comes amid fierce competition from AI agents from Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Elon Musk’s Grok. 
  • Apple posted new job listings to hire senior engineers to design AI agents to execute multistep tasks across apps, browsers, coding tools, and operating systems.
  • Apple’s move comes in the wake of strong demand seen for Meta’s Muse AI agent.

Apple (AAPL) is recruiting talent to build an independent artificial intelligence agent that can handle complex tasks for users, signaling a push into a crowded market already populated by OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and other tech players.

Fresh career postings on Apple's site this week shed new light on the project, Bloomberg first reported. One opening seeks a senior engineering manager to help turn foundational work into building a proactive assistant capable of browsing websites, working across applications, running commands, writing and debugging software code, and invoking external services.

AAPL stock gained about 0.4% after-hours, while Meta Platforms (META), which runs Muse AI, and newly listed Anthropic (ANT) eased 1.8% after-hours.

The project is still in its early phases, though Apple has looked at a potential rollout as early as late 2027.

A Crowded Field 

Apple's move comes as rival AI agents gain rapid traction among consumers and developers. Meta's Muse has drawn wide attention for handling tasks such as booking travel, reserving tables at restaurants, and putting together news summaries.

Meta’s Muse, in a few days since launch, topped the charts for mobile app downloads.

Similar to Meta, other AI labs and tech peers have either launched or begun testing their customer-focused AI products. Anthropic expanded user testing for Duet, OpenAI broadened Dots, and Google revamped its agent into Tasks earlier this week.

Agentic apps have claimed prominent spots on Apple's App Store, with Muse holding the No. 2 spot among free apps on Thursday just behind TikTok, and ChatGPT and Claude ranking inside the top five.

Apple Emphasizes Privacy Guardrails 

Apple noted in its job descriptions that systems capable of executing code, accessing credentials, and acting on behalf of users require strict permission controls, transparency, and sandboxing.

Separately, Apple is broadening Siri's integration with third-party apps in the upcoming iOS 27.3 release to support actions like booking a ride or a restaurant table.

AAPL Stock: Retail View 

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘bearish’ with ‘low’ message volumes.

AAPL stock has gained about 28% year-to-date.

data.title: Record profits but record outflows: 'Sell Korea' trade stalks Seoul market
data.description:
Key points:
  • KOSPI down 44% from June's record high, remains up 20% year-to-date
  • Record profits at Samsung and SK Hynix no panacea as buybacks dry up
  • Equity outflows stretch to seventh month, drawdown eclipses any since 2008

By Gregor Stuart Hunter and Heekyong Yang

South Korea's biggest companies are posting record AI-driven profits and the stock market is among the world's cheapest, yet foreign investors keep heading for the exits — and with buybacks winding down, few buyers are left to step in.

No major equity index rode the AI boom harder than Seoul's KOSPI , which hit a record in June but has since lost 44%, wiping out some 3.3 quadrillion won ($2.4 trillion) in market value as doubts grow over the debt-fuelled AI infrastructure buildout.

That's even as earnings vaulted ninefold and sevenfold, respectively, to unprecedented levels at Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix , the dominant makers globally of the AI memory chips needed by data centres. Together, the companies make up nearly half the KOSPI's value.

It demonstrates a disconnect in the market, which analysts say is now driven less by corporate fundamentals than by a lack of buyers, and points to a swift loss of conviction among investors for the chipmakers at the heart of the AI trade.

"We're essentially experiencing a full-fledged 'Sell Korea' trend," said Han Jiyoung, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities in Seoul.

"The challenge for the market now is to find a catalyst that could bring foreign investors back."

Foreigners are on course to sell Korean stocks for a seventh straight month in November, with cumulative net outflows of $115.2 billion marking the biggest retreat on record in LSEG data to the start of 2008.

Overseas purchases of leveraged single-stock ETFs, particularly ones tied to SK Hynix in Hong Kong , fuelled outsized gains on the way up, but ultimately accelerated the speed and depth of the rout.

Corporate share buybacks, which had soaked up much of the foreign selling in recent months, are also easing off. Retail investors, who are still nursing losses from a wrenching selloff that started in June, may struggle to fill the gap.

FUNDAMENTALS VS FLOWS

Record profits at South Korea's two biggest firms have resulted in eye-popping shareholder-return plans for 2026, worth as much as 210 trillion won combined, including buybacks, dividends and share cancellations. But with the end of those programs approaching, markets are on edge.

Responding to Reuters questions on Thursday, Samsung Electronics reiterated plans to return up to 110 trillion won to shareholders for 2026, saying its board would finalise the scale and execution of the remaining returns in late January.

SK Hynix also reaffirmed plans to return about 100 trillion won to shareholders through share buybacks and cancellations, adding that it would continue quarterly share repurchases and pay special dividends on significant investment gains.

The sentiment around the AI trade has worsened markedly in recent weeks, after the emphatic victory by Democrats in this month's US midterms fuelled worries about a slowdown in data-centre construction. Washington's restrictions on advanced chip supply to several US trading partners in Asia and Latin America have exacerbated worries further.

"There's a capitulation, where positions are shifting away from anything linked to AI into anything defensive, high quality and stable," said Isaac Thong, a portfolio manager at the Aberdeen Asian Income Fund in Singapore.

"Why it doesn't feel like previous down cycles is because fundamentally things are still really strong in the AI world," he said. "There's a lot of confidence at a corporate level, at least in the shorter term."

Last month, Samsung said chip supplies were expected to remain tight through 2028, while SK Hynix painted a similarly bullish picture of demand, pointing to an even longer supply crunch.

Goldman Sachs lowered its target on the KOSPI this week for the second time since the end of October, to 7,500 from 12,000, "to account for the market’s continued reluctance to fully price in fundamentals."

"We still see Korea offering the greatest potential upside among regional markets," Goldman strategists said. The KOSPI closed at 5,062.92 on Wednesday, still up 20% this year in local currency terms.

Korean stocks trade at a substantial discount to global peers, with MSCI's country gauge trading at a multiple of 3.27 times forward earnings, compared to 15.35 times for the MSCI All-Country World index, according to LSEG Datastream.

Tighter regulation and other guardrails after the US midterms could eventually raise costs and slow the AI buildout, according to Seoul-based Sanjeev Rana, head of North Asia semiconductor research at CLSA.

But given how important AI infrastructure is to the US economy and jobs, Rana expects most of the capacity needed to support AI's growth to be built, even if the pace slows or other countries take up the slack.

In the medium term, "the elections and the changing political landscape doesn't change the outlook in any meaningful way," he said.

"Earnings for 2027 are still pretty much in the bag."

data.title: Xi faced Trump with weak economic hand: McGeever
data.description:
By Jamie McGeever

US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping held their third official meeting of the year on Thursday, in Shenzhen. While much attention has focused on the US leader’s recent setbacks, his host also came to the talks with a weakening economic hand.

Many of the issues that curbed Trump's swagger in May and even September, such as sticky inflation, high borrowing costs and dismal approval ratings, were still burning when he met Xi in Shenzhen on Thursday. The Republican Party's historic beating in the recent US midterm elections testifies to that. Meanwhile, the scandal surrounding Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, including potential investigations into the AI giant, is a major headache that Trump could do without.

But none of that automatically implies Xi holds the stronger economic cards today, as he appeared to in May. Back then, there were signs that China might finally be emerging from the deflationary doom loop triggered by its property crash that began in 2020-21, the biggest real estate bust in history.

China’s domestic economic activity, especially retail sales, industrial production, and business investment, was picking up, and the country’s economic surprises index had just hit its highest point in three years. Annual consumer inflation had leapt to a three-year high, and producer disinflation was at its lowest level for 18 months.

Six months on, those flickering embers of recovery have been snuffed out.

AI EXPORTS SURGE

The latest official figures from Beijing show the world's second-largest economy has not broken free from that deflationary spiral: lending, spending and investment all remain weak. The deflationary gloom is also infecting investor sentiment. The stock market has fallen more than 20% since the summer, Hong Kong tech stocks are at a more than two-year nadir, and China's 10-year bond yield is at a record low.

The one bright spot remains exports. Record shipments abroad, increasingly of high-tech products, semiconductors, integrated circuits, converters, and storage batteries, delivered a trade surplus of more than $1 trillion last year, a feat that has already been repeated this year.

Thanks to net trade, Beijing is on track to meet its 4.5%-5.0% annual growth target for 2026. Analysts estimate that net exports contributed around 2 percentage points to the wider economy's 4.5% annual growth rate in the third quarter. That's unusually large, especially for such a big economy.

But what if the AI bubble deflates or, even worse, bursts?

ACHILLES’ HEEL

Of course, it is in both Trump's and Xi's interests that it doesn't. AI spending is vital for growth in the world’s two largest economies, as is controlling the flow of equipment, materials and resources needed for the AI buildout. Both leaders are committed to "winning" the AI arms race.

But because AI is so important to both countries, it is also a potential Achilles’ heel. In the US, an AI slowdown — and subsequent market correction — could weigh on growth significantly, both directly and through negative wealth effects. But the risk is arguably greater for China because of the country’s domestic frailty.

There are many indicators highlighting China’s weakness at home, but none captures it better than fixed asset investment, which is falling at its fastest pace since the pandemic.

In fact, excluding that distorted period, fixed investment in China is falling at the fastest pace since comparable records began 30 years ago.

'UNINVESTIBLE?'

So how might that affect the balance of power between Trump and Xi?

There's a school of thought, supported by Louis-Vincent Gave, founding partner of Gavekal Research, that Washington will have to thaw icy trade ties with Beijing if it wants to lower its own interest burden and inflation. "China remains the one deflationary force in the world today," Gave said in a podcast last month. "If you want to get inflation down, you have no choice but to embrace China."

Perhaps. But it doesn't jibe with the Trump administration’s consideration of new restrictions on US firms using Chinese AI models, not to mention its tightening curbs on China’s access to US-developed AI chips.

In 2023, then-US Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo said American firms had told her that China was "uninvestible." Her unusually blunt remark angered Beijing and created a diplomatic storm at the time. The validity of her claim remains highly debatable, but China's economy is surely not as investible as Xi would like it to be.

(The opinions expressed here are those of Jamie McGeever, a columnist for Reuters)

And listen to the Morning Bid daily podcast on Apple, Spotify, or the Reuters app. Subscribe to hear Reuters journalists discuss the biggest news in markets and finance seven days a week.

data.title: CareScout Focuses Strategic Direction on Aging Care Services
data.description:
CareScout today announced a singular focus on its aging care services business and plans to discontinue new insurance sales through CareScout Insurance Company in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements.

The decision reflects CareScout’s belief that its services business offers the greatest opportunity to help millions of families navigate aging care for their loved ones and create long-term value for Genworth shareholders.

“We set out to make the aging journey more confident, connected, and clear, and that ambition has not changed,” said Samir Shah, CEO of CareScout. “We are choosing to focus our investment on a capital-light services business where we see the greatest opportunity for growth and long-term value creation. Together with our partners, we can help more families plan for and manage the care of aging loved ones as their needs evolve.”

CareScout brings together cost-of-care insights, care expertise, personalized guidance, and access to quality care to help families understand their needs, explore their options, and take the next steps with confidence. Building on these capabilities, the company will work with insurers, employers, advisors, and care providers to reach more families and broaden its services across the aging journey.

Existing CareScout Insurance policies remain in force with no change to servicing contacts or processes, and CareScout Insurance Company remains committed to meeting all contractual obligations. The decision is not expected to have a material impact on Genworth’s financial condition or results of operations.

data.title: Midland States to Sell, Combine Branches With Strategic Plan
data.description:
By Natalie Weger

Midland States Bancorp plans to sell six branches and to combine two additional branches into nearby locations as part of a new strategic plan.

The plan is intended to optimize the community bank's branch network based on customer banking patterns, market presence and proximity to other Midland locations.

As part of the plan, United Bank of Union will acquire the company's Missouri branch, and then both Constitute Bank and Longview Community Bank will acquire separate Illinois branches.

Those sales include the transfer of deposits totaling $156.3 million and loans associated with the branches totaling $1.5 million, as of Sept. 30, 2026. The branch sales are expected to close by the end of the first quarter of 2027.

Separately, Midland States plans to combine two Illinois branches into nearby bank branches during the first quarter of 2027. Following the changes, the bank would operate 45 branch locations.

Write to Natalie Weger at natalie.weger@wsj.com.

data.title: Rally May Stall For Japan Stock Market
data.description:
TOKYO (dpa-AFX) - The Japan stock market has tracked higher in consecutive trading days, climbing more than 580 points or 1 percent along the way. The Nikkei 225 now sits just beneath the 59,450-point plateau although it may spin its wheels on Friday.

The global forecast for the Asian markets is weak on continuing AI concerns and rising crude oil prices. The European and U.S. markets were down and the Asian bourses are expected to open in similar fashion.

The Nikkei finished modestly higher on Thursday following gains from the technology, finance, property and textile companies.

For the day, the index advanced 419.93 points or 0.71 percent to finish at 59,444.21 after trading between 58,750.53 and 59,660.61.

The lead from Wall Street is broadly negative as the major averages opened slightly higher on Thursday but quickly turned lower and continued to accelerate to the downside throughout the session, ending at daily lows.

The Dow plunged 1,101.11 points or 2.19 percent to finish at 49,097.06, while the NASDAQ tumbled 550.69 points or 2.25 percent to close at 23,879.20 and the S&P 500 crashed 147.80 points or 2.02 percent to end at 7,175.83.

The markets initially benefited from a positive reaction to artificial intelligence company Anthropic's (ANT) initial public offering. Buying interest waned shortly after the start of trading, however, and selling pressure intensified soon after intelligence company Anthropic made its debut on the NASDAQ.

While the Claude developer priced its initial public offering at a higher-than-expected $83 per share and soared by nearly 40 percent as it began trading, the stock pulled back well off its highs as the day progressed. The pullback by Anthropic and the sell-off was attributed to profit taking amid lingering concerns about where the AI trade goes from here.

In U.S. economic news, the Labor Department released a report showing first-time claims for U.S. unemployment benefits unexpectedly edged higher last week.

Crude oil prices edged higher on Thursday as fears of supply disruptions increased in the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate crude for December delivery was up $0.17 or 0.20 percent at $83.43 per barrel.

Closer to home, Japan will release October figures for consumer prices later this morning. Overall national inflation was flat on month and up 2.1 percent on year in September, while core CPI also rose an annual 2.1 percent.

data.title: Vection Technologies Proposes zSpace Acquisition And $5m Placement
data.description:
Vection Technologies is proposing to acquire US education technology business zSpace for approximately US$9.5 million in a predominantly share-funded transaction.

The Australian technology group also has plans for a simultaneous A$5m placement to support the acquisition, provide working capital, and fund integration and sales expansion.

The proposed combination would bring together Vection’s AI and extended reality (XR) products with zSpace’s customer network spanning more than 3,500 US school districts.

Completion remains conditional on financing, creditor arrangements, litigation outcomes, and other approvals, while the capital raising is not conditional on the acquisition proceeding.

Share-Based Consideration

Vection proposes to acquire all of zSpace through a cash-out merger, with approximately US$9.2m payable in Vection shares to principal creditors and sellers 3i, Fiza and Itria.

That consideration includes US$5.43m in shares at settlement and US$3.79m deferred across four quarterly tranches, with pricing floors and market-based adjustments.

Approximately US$0.3m in cash would be used to acquire the remaining public shareholding, while up to US$3.5m of further performance-based consideration may become payable.

The proposed A$5m placement is priced at 1.0575 cents a share, a 24.5% discount to the 15-day volume-weighted average price, with one attaching option for every two shares subject to shareholder approval.

Vection has separately outlined a secured bridge facility of up to US$5m for zSpace, with further drawdowns at its discretion and an initial US$350,000 advance.

Education Network Reach

zSpace supplies headset-free three-dimensional learning computers and curriculum content for science, technology, engineering and mathematics, and career-focused education.

Its installed footprint includes more than 20,000 Inspire units, while renewable software contracts had an annualised value of US$9.4m at 30 June 2026.

The business generated US$27.9m of revenue in calendar 2025, although revenue declined to US$10.6m in the first half of 2026 from US$14.2m a year earlier.

Vection recorded A$39.8m in revenue from contracts and A$6m in underlying EBITDA for the year ended June 2026.

Combining those results with zSpace’s latest 12-month revenue produces an illustrative A$74.5m revenue base, but the figures are unaudited, exclude acquisition accounting and do not constitute a forecast.

Turnaround Risks Remain

Vection intends to distribute its Algho AI tools and 3DFrame content through zSpace’s education channel, with a joint 21-product roadmap beginning in March 2027.

Management is targeting more than A$100m in combined annual revenue by 2028, an ambition dependent on improved zSpace trading, cost savings and cross-selling rather than contracted sales.

zSpace remained loss-making in the first half of 2026, with its financial statements identifying substantial doubt about its ability to continue operating.

The acquisition also depends on the outcome of litigation brought by EdtechX, scheduled for trial in January 2027, alongside the proposed restructuring of existing debt and other conditions.

If the acquisition does not proceed, Vection may redirect placement funds to alternative acquisitions or general working capital, while interim advances to zSpace carry recovery risk.
